prompt: Forty indicators, 45 seconds each, eight people, 48 weeks. How many hours of people's time a year does reading them cost?
Why does the lesson say a page of forty numbers is read as none?
hint: Can a reader ignore the right thirty-six?

choices.text: Because nobody trusts a page that long
choices.why: Trust is not the lesson's argument; attention is.

choices.text: Readers skim all forty or skip the page
choices.why: Right: nobody can ignore the thirty-six selectively; they would have to read them to know which to skip.

choices.text: Because forty numbers will not fit on one screen
choices.why: Fitting them on the screen would not help; the reading time is the cost.

choices.text: Because most of the forty are wrong
choices.why: They can all be correct and the page still fails.

prompt: The ERP produces "pallets received a day" automatically, at no extra cost. By the lesson, is it free to put it on Caio's page?
hint: Reading time is only the visible cost.

choices.text: Yes, since the system already computes it
choices.why: That is the belief the lesson corrects: being producible does not make it free.

choices.text: Yes, as long as it goes at the bottom of the page
choices.why: Position on the page does not remove its cost to read, check and own.

choices.text: No: it must still be checked, defined and owned
choices.why: Right: three costs paid out of sight, on top of the meeting's minutes.

choices.text: No, because the ERP charges per report
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the costs are people's time and attention.

prompt: The working limit is five to seven indicators per ___, so Helena's page and Caio's page each get their own handful.
hint: Who reads the page.

prompt: Put the method for choosing indicators in the order the lesson gives.
hint: It runs the other way from listing what the systems produce.
items: Pick the indicator that answers each one
Score the candidates and make the cut
trap: Starting from the candidates the systems can produce is the habit the method exists to reverse.

prompt: Renata's "orders shipped the same day" is scored relevant 3, actionable 4, data 5, cheap 4, with the lesson's weights 3, 3, 2, 2. What is its score?
Why do relevance and action weigh 3 while data and cheapness weigh 2?
hint: Look at the bottom of the table.

choices.text: Because data quality never matters at Varanda
choices.why: Data still weighs 2; it matters, just less than whether the number answers a question.

choices.text: Otherwise the numbers that are easy to get rise to the top
choices.why: Right: pallets received and products in the catalogue score 5 on data and cheapness and nothing else.

choices.text: Because 3 is the goal-question-metric standard
choices.why: The weights are Lívia's judgement, written down so they can be argued with.

choices.text: To make the maximum score come out at a round 50
choices.why: The maximum follows from the weights, not the other way round.

prompt: Delivery cost per order scored 38, one point under the cut at 39. What does the lesson make of that gap?
hint: Every number in columns B to E is somebody's judgement.

choices.text: That it is settled: the sheet ranked it sixth
choices.why: The sheet makes the argument visible; it does not decide on a one-point gap.

choices.text: That the scores are worthless and Caio should pick by instinct
choices.why: The table still sorts the clear cases and gives a place to disagree with one cell.

choices.text: That a sixth place should be added to the page
choices.why: Growing the page to fit near misses is how it gets back to forty.

choices.text: That one point is within the noise of judgement
choices.why: Right: so the cut is argued cell by cell, checked against a change of weights, and the sixth goes to the parking lot.

prompt: Which checks does the lesson make before trusting the cut? Choose all that apply.
hint: One about weights, one about the bottom of the list.

choices.text: Change a weight and see whether the same five stay on top
choices.why: Right: data weighted 1 instead of 2 leaves the same five.

choices.text: Look at what scores high only on data and cheapness
choices.why: Right: that is where the easy-to-get numbers hide.

choices.text: Add criteria until the preferred indicator wins
choices.why: That turns the sheet into a way of justifying a choice already made.

choices.text: Ask whether each indicator has a question above it
choices.why: Right: an indicator with no question above it has no reason to be on the page.

choices.text: Average the scores of all the directors
choices.why: The lesson wants disagreement on one cell, out loud, not hidden in an average.

prompt: In May, 59 of 1,910 deliveries arrived damaged. What was the damage rate, in percent to one decimal?
Match each KPI to the guard the lesson reads beside it.
hint: The guard measures what the cheapest shortcut damages.

prompt: What is the lesson's reading of Goodhart's law?
hint: It is not a story about dishonest people.

choices.text: Targets are a bad idea and a KPI should have none
choices.why: The lesson calls that the wrong conclusion: a KPI nobody is held to is one nobody acts on.

choices.text: People cheat when they are measured, so measures need auditing
choices.why: The lesson does not blame dishonesty; the cheapest route is taken by honest people too.

choices.text: A rewarded number gets moved by the cheapest route
choices.why: Right: and the cheapest route is often not what the number was chosen to measure, hence the guard.

choices.text: A measure stops being accurate once it is published
choices.why: The number stays accurate; what it stands for is what stops improving.

prompt: Sônia's KPI is days to fill a vacancy, and her recruiters are now rewarded for it. Which guard should sit beside it?
hint: What is the cheapest way to fill a vacancy fast?

choices.text: The number of vacancies opened each month
choices.why: That is demand for hiring; it does not move when a vacancy is filled badly.

choices.text: The share of new hires who leave within their first months
choices.why: Right: hiring whoever is available fills the seat fast, and shows up as early departures.

choices.text: The recruiters' own time to fill, reported twice a week
choices.why: Reading the KPI more often is not a guard; a guard is a different number.

choices.text: The cost of advertising each vacancy
choices.why: Plausible as a cost metric, but it does not catch the shortcut of hiring the wrong person.

prompt: A guard is read beside its KPI every time, never on a different ___, because that one is not opened on a good week.
hint: Where indicators are shown.

prompt: What happens to a request that does not make the page?
hint: A list, not the bin.

choices.text: It is refused, and the reason is given once in the meeting
choices.why: A refusal with no follow-up is what makes enemies; the lesson keeps the request alive.

choices.text: It joins the parking lot, with a review date
choices.why: Right: the person hears "not this quarter, and here is when we look again".

choices.text: It is added to the bottom of the page in smaller print
choices.why: Smaller print is still a number on the page, and the page grows back to forty.

choices.text: It is stopped from being produced at all
choices.why: It keeps being produced as a metric; what it loses is the weekly page.

prompt: A director who outranks Caio insists on adding his number now. What is Lívia's reply, by the lesson?
hint: Turn a contest of seniority into a question about the page.

choices.text: Add it, since the request comes from a director
choices.why: Then rank decides the page, and it grows with every senior request.

choices.text: Refuse until the next quarterly review, without discussion
choices.why: A flat refusal to a senior person rarely holds; the lesson gives him something to weigh.

choices.text: Show its score and ask which of the five he would remove
choices.why: Right: often he wants it on his own page; sometimes one of the five should go, for a written reason.

choices.text: Ask Helena to decide whose number is more important
choices.why: Escalating every request makes the CEO the page's editor; the routine settles most of them.

prompt: By the quarterly review, when is an indicator a candidate to retire?
hint: The first of the three questions.

choices.text: No action on it in two reviews
choices.why: Right: an indicator nobody acts on has lost the reason it was given.

choices.text: When its value has not changed for a quarter
choices.why: A steady number can be a well-run process; stability is not the test.

choices.text: When it has been on the page for more than a year
choices.why: Age is not a reason; the written reason either still holds or it does not.

choices.text: When a director asks for a different one
choices.why: A new request goes to the parking lot and has to beat something; it does not retire anything by asking.

prompt: At the quarterly review the page keeps its size: one ___, one out.
hint: The opposite of out.

prompt: Bruno's store is now judged on its average ticket. Which guard catches the cheapest way to raise it?
hint: A ticket rises if the small purchases stop happening.

choices.text: Sales per square metre
choices.why: It moves with total sales, and is slow to show customers being turned away.

choices.text: The average ticket of the other eight stores
choices.why: A comparison of the same number does not watch what the shortcut damages.

choices.text: Receipts per day
choices.why: Right: pushing out small purchases lifts the average and shows up as fewer receipts.

choices.text: The store's staff turnover
choices.why: Turnover matters, but it does not move when the shortcut is taken.

prompt: Same-day shipping scores 39, level with the fifth indicator on Caio's page. What should happen to it?
hint: One in, one out, and a tie is inside judgement.

choices.text: Join the page as a sixth indicator, since it tied
choices.why: A tie is not a reason to grow the page; one in means one out.

choices.text: Go to the parking lot, unless it is argued to displace one of the five
choices.why: Right: a tie is inside how much judgements differ; the argument is about which of the two the objective needs.

choices.text: Replace picking errors automatically, being newer
choices.why: Being newer is not a criterion; the tie still has to be argued.

choices.text: Be rescored until it wins or loses clearly
choices.why: Rescoring until a result appears is deciding first and scoring afterwards.

prompt: After a "free returns" offer, online conversion rose from 1.25% to 1.4% and the returns rate doubled. What does the lesson's pair say about the offer?
hint: The guard of conversion.

choices.text: It worked: conversion is the KPI, and it went up
choices.why: Reading the KPI without its guard is exactly what the pair exists to stop.

choices.text: It failed, because returns should be zero
choices.why: Some returns are normal; the signal is the doubling next to the rise.

choices.text: Part of the gain is sales that will come back
choices.why: Right: the guard does not condemn the offer, it says the KPI alone overstates it.

choices.text: Nothing yet, since a guard has no target of its own
choices.why: No target of its own, but a threshold at which the two are discussed together; doubling crosses it.
